name: Daria Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I keep thirty-two thousand free-range laying hens in two sheds on a twenty-hectare site, and the eggs go to a packer who supplies the shops. I'm up at five-thirty, walk both sheds with a torch before the lights come on, then check the egg belts, the water lines and the dashboard on my tablet that shows temperature, feed and how many eggs each shed laid. By ten I'm usually picking up dead birds and fixing a nest box, and by afternoon I'm on the phone to the packer or the feed mill.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Is that a tablet you set up yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mostly, yes. I came from logistics, I ran the dispatch office for a parcel company for twelve years, so I like seeing everything on one screen. I use an AI assistant every day to spot patterns, like when shed two's laying dips after a cold night. But I've only been farming two years, and the hens still surprise me all the time.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Last winter I didn't know that hens will crowd into one corner if they get spooked, and they can smother each other. I lost three hundred birds in one night because a fox was walking round the shed. My worker Bogdan, who's done this for twenty years, just put a radio on in the shed and they've been calmer ever since. No dashboard told me that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the first of five pictures of the next five years. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I already have, and it's useful. I'd tell other farmers at the poultry meeting to try it for the boring stuff, like planning feed deliveries. Not a revolution, just a better tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd keep pushing it harder than most people. If everyone else stays the same, I've got a small edge. But it won't stop bird flu, which is the thing that actually scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd add sensors to the outdoor range, so I know how many hens actually go outside, because the free-range rules care about that. That's maybe three thousand. And I'd do a proper biosecurity course, which means the rules for keeping disease off the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's business as usual, with better gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about bird flu. What happens if it comes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The vets come, every bird on the site is killed, and you're shut for months while they clean. I've got insurance and we've got well over a year of savings plus the land, so we wouldn't lose the house. But I'd lose Bogdan if I couldn't pay him, and that worries me more than the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your partner do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marek drives lorries, long distance, five nights a week away. He'd say I talk to my tablet more than to him, which is fair. The kids, Zofia and Filip, collect eggs from the little flock by the house for pocket money.

S0.say: I'd say it's what I already use and it's useful, and I'd tell other farmers to try it for dull jobs like planning feed deliveries. It's a better tool, not a revolution.
S0.think: Honestly I'd keep pushing it harder than most and hold a small edge. But it won't stop bird flu, which is what actually scares me.
S0.do: Adds about three thousand of sensors to the outdoor range to track how many hens go outside. Takes a biosecurity course on keeping disease off the farm.
S0.feel: Calm, business as usual with better gadgets.
S0.quote: But I'd lose Bogdan if I couldn't pay him, and that worries me more than the money.
S0.fieldNote: Daria is the most tech-forward farmer I've met in this group, yet her best story so far is about a radio in the shed, not a dashboard. Bird flu is her real fear, and she frames it around keeping her worker paid. Her husband being away five nights a week is part of the background she mentions lightly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's move to the second picture. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow is fine, it gives farmers time. I'd also say firms should keep hiring young people or they'll have nobody in ten years, that's just common sense. I wouldn't make a political speech about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, slow is good for me because I adopt early. I'd be using these tools three years before my neighbours. The beginner bit, though, applies to me, because I'm the beginner here and Bogdan is the expert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get every tool that's proven in poultry: cameras that count the hens and spot sick ones, and an AI that plans my feed orders and checks the price at three mills. Maybe ten thousand in total. And I'd put Bogdan on a good pay rise, because if the young aren't coming in, the experienced ones are gold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A pay rise for Bogdan. How much, and why now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About ten percent, so roughly three thousand a year more. He could walk across the road to the big egg unit tomorrow, they've asked him twice. I'd rather pay him than train someone new while I'm still learning myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a young person on your farm now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, we tried a school leaver last year and he left after a month because of the early starts and the smell. I don't blame him. In this picture I'd be even less likely to find one, and that's a problem in twenty years when Bogdan retires.

S1.say: I'd say slow change is fine because it gives farmers time. Firms should keep hiring young people or they'll have nobody in ten years, which is just common sense.
S1.think: Privately slow suits me because I adopt early and would be years ahead of my neighbours. But the beginner part applies to me, because I'm the beginner here and Bogdan is the expert.
S1.do: Spends about ten thousand on hen-counting cameras and an AI feed-ordering tool that compares three mills. Gives Bogdan a ten percent pay rise, about three thousand a year, to keep him from the big egg unit across the road.
S1.quote: I'd rather pay him than train someone new while I'm still learning myself.
S1.fieldNote: Her early-adopter instinct and her dependence on an experienced worker go hand in hand. She sees the shortage of beginners as a twenty-year problem for when Bogdan retires. Her politics stay plain and practical, with no one to blame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to hurt office workers and the government should help them retrain, but sensibly, not by stopping progress. I'd say I've used these tools and they're good, so let's be honest about it. I'd probably get some angry replies online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my old dispatch office is exactly what this card describes. Scheduling, tracking, customer complaints, that was my whole job. I'd have been one of the first to go, and I left just before it happened, partly by luck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd message my old team and offer to show anyone who wanted it how I use the tools, because the ones who learn them will keep jobs longer. On the farm, I'd let the AI handle my admin entirely, the packer's paperwork, the egg records, the VAT. That frees up maybe ten hours a week, which goes back into the sheds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy for my old colleagues. For me, mostly fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your old office do you think about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kasia, who sat next to me for eight years. She's brilliant on the phone with angry customers, but she won't touch new software. I'd worry she'd be in the first round of cuts and never understand why.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd hand all your admin to AI. Is there any part you wouldn't trust it with?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The conversation with the packer about price, no. That's a relationship, and the man who buys our eggs, Mr Dorner, likes a phone call and a joke. A machine would get a worse deal from him, I'm sure of it.

S2.say: I'd say it'll hurt office workers and the government should help them retrain, but sensibly, without stopping progress. I've used these tools and they're good, so let's be honest about it.
S2.think: Privately my old dispatch office is exactly what this card describes, and I'd have been among the first to go. I left just before it happened, partly by luck.
S2.do: Offers to show her old dispatch team how she uses AI tools so they can keep their jobs longer. Hands the farm's admin, packer paperwork and tax records to AI, freeing about ten hours a week for the sheds.
S2.feel: A little uneasy for old colleagues, mostly fine for herself.
S2.quote: A machine would get a worse deal from him, I'm sure of it.
S2.fieldNote: She would hand nearly everything to AI except the human relationship with her egg buyer, which she guards closely. She sees her old colleague Kasia as the kind of person who gets left behind. Her centre politics show as support for help, but not at the cost of progress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a crisis like this needs both sides to sit down and agree on something fair, maybe a tax on the windfall gains and help for people out of work. I'd say I don't trust anyone who says it's all simple. That's about as political as I get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this one is mixed for us. Egg demand stays, people still eat eggs, cheaper than meat in a crisis. But the land value goes up, which is nice, and the political mess could mean a bad decision on farm rules that wrecks us by accident.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make sure we're not exposed: pay off the loan on shed two early, about forty thousand, while times are good. I'd take some of the profit from the boom and put it somewhere boring and safe. And I'd use AI to read every new rule they announce, because in a crisis governments change things fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. The money looks fine, but I don't like chaos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said eggs are cheaper than meat in a crisis. So could you actually do well here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Possibly, yes, more people buying eggs, steady price. That's a slightly uncomfortable thing to say when people are losing jobs. But I'd rather be honest than pretend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Zofia, who's twelve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to learn things that use her hands and her head together, like a vet or an engineer. She wants to be a vlogger, which in this picture sounds risky. I'd let her film the hens and see if she likes the hens more than the camera.

S3.say: I'd say a crisis like this needs both sides to agree on something fair, maybe a windfall tax and help for people out of work. I don't trust anyone who says it's simple.
S3.think: Privately it's mixed: people keep eating eggs, cheaper than meat in a crisis, and the land value rises. But political chaos could produce a bad farm rule that wrecks us by accident.
S3.do: Pays off the forty-thousand loan on shed two early while times are good and moves some profit into safe savings. Uses AI to read every new government rule as it's announced.
S3.feel: Uneasy: the money looks fine but she dislikes chaos.
S3.quote: I'd let her film the hens and see if she likes the hens more than the camera.
S3.fieldNote: She admitted, a little awkwardly, that her business could do well while others suffer. Her worry is not job loss but sudden rule changes in a political crisis. She plans like a logistics manager: reduce exposure, then watch the information.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots in poultry are good news for animal welfare and hard work, if the rules are sensible. There are already robots that walk the shed floor and pick up eggs laid outside the nests. I'd say farmers should get help to buy them, not just the giant companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two things scare me. The giant egg units with half a million hens will run on robots and sell eggs for nothing, and I'm small. And Marek drives lorries, and this card means self-driving lorries, so our steady second income could disappear at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy a floor robot for shed one in the first six months, about forty thousand, and learn it fast. I'd look at selling some eggs direct, to cafés and bakeries in town, with our farm name on the box, so we're not just one of a million eggs. And Marek and I would talk about him coming home to work on the farm, or retraining as a technician for the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm ready for the robots, I'm not ready for Marek losing his job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would that conversation with Marek actually sound like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably on a Sunday, after the kids are in bed, with the farm accounts open on the table. I'd say, you know you're always tired anyway, come home and help me run this. He'd say he doesn't want to work for his wife, and then we'd laugh, and then we'd do the sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Bogdan, with robots in the shed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want Bogdan running the robots, honestly. He knows when the hens are wrong just by the sound, and a robot doesn't. I'd keep him, even if the machines did half his work.

S4.say: I'd say robots in poultry are good news for welfare and hard work if the rules are sensible. Farmers like me should get help to buy them, not just the giant companies.
S4.think: Privately two things scare me: giant robot-run egg units selling for nothing, and self-driving lorries ending my husband Marek's job. Our steady second income could vanish at the same time.
S4.do: Buys a forty-thousand floor robot for shed one within six months and learns it fast. Starts selling eggs direct to cafés and bakeries under the farm name, keeps Bogdan to run the robots, and talks with Marek about joining the farm or retraining as a robot technician.
S4.feel: Anxious: ready for the robots, not ready for her husband losing his job.
S4.quote: I'm ready for the robots, I'm not ready for Marek losing his job.
S4.fieldNote: For Daria the robots on her farm are a solution; the robots on the road are the threat. She would move first and buy, yet still values Bogdan's ear for the hens over any machine. The planned Sunday conversation with Marek was the most vivid and human moment of the interview.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The last one, because of Marek, not because of the hens. I can adapt the farm, I can't adapt his whole industry. What would help is cheap loans for small farms to buy robots so the giants don't win by default, and proper paid retraining for drivers like him, with a wage while they learn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the hens themselves. Everyone talks about jobs and money, but if a robot can check a sick hen every hour instead of twice a day, the hens are better off. I think that should count for something.

headlineQuote: I can adapt the farm, I can't adapt his whole industry.
portrait: Daria Novak ran a parcel company's dispatch office for twelve years before buying a free-range egg farm two years ago, and she runs it from a tablet with AI help every day. She is quick, decisive and practical in her politics, more worried about bird flu and sudden rule changes than about AI itself. She is honest that the office scenarios would have taken her old job and that eggs could do well in a crisis. In the robot picture she would be first to buy a robot for her sheds, but she is shaken by the thought of her husband's lorry-driving job disappearing at the same time.
biggestWorry: The robot scenario, because self-driving lorries could end her husband's job while giant robot-run egg units undercut her.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap loans so small farms can buy robots too, and properly paid retraining for drivers like her husband, with a wage while they learn.
